newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: German 'superspy' to be freed from Colombia jail.
newsitem.headline: German 'superspy' to be freed from Colombia jail.

text.p: Jailed German "superspy" Werner Mauss and his wife, Michaela, were expected to be released on Friday night from the Colombian prison where they had been awaiting trial on kidnap-related charges, their lawyer said.

Abraham Casallas told Reuters the German duo, who were captured near the northwest city of Medellin in mid-November last year as they tried to bundle a German kidnap victim aboard a plane out of the country, could be free before midnight or early on Saturday.
He said the Mausses would still face trial but would be released "without conditions" under the terms of a habeas corpus appeal that was granted by a judge in Medellin.
"There were irregularities in the case against them. The trial will continue but they will be free unconditionally," Casallas said by phone from the Medellin jail where Werner Mauss is being held.
"They will not be allowed out of the country until the legal case is resolved," he added.
Mauss and his wife were originally charged with kidnap and conspiracy to abduct Brigitte Schoene, the wife of a Medellin- based former BASF Chemicals executive, and a number of lesser charges.

All but two charges were later dropped, leaving the couple facing only accusations of using false documents and seeking personal benefit from abduction -- a reference to seeking payment in return for freeing a kidnap victim.
Schoene was kidnapped last year by suspected rebels of the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second-largest guerrilla group.
Regional authorities claimed the Mausses were international members of the ELN or mercenaries who negotiated the freedom of kidnap victims in return for a cut of the ransom.

Mauss was briefly linked to Germany's secret services and has close ties with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's head of intelligence services, leading both the German and Colombian media to dub him a James Bond-style superagent.

When the couple was captured, German diplomats said they were working on a "humanitarian mission" in Colombia with their full consent. It later emerged that the German authorities had knowingly granted the pair passports under false names.
It was not immediately known where the Mausses would stay on their release from jail.
